steps.tx: Tuberculous spondylitis, universally known as **Pott's spine**, was originally described by Percivall Pott in 1779 and accounts for more than fifty percent of all cases of musculoskeletal tuberculosis. Haematogenous seeding via the Batson perivertebral venous plexus or anterior spinal arterial arcades implants Mycobacterium tuberculosis into the rich cancellous bone of the anterior paradiscal vertebral body.
steps.say: Pott spine or tuberculous spondylodiscitis accounts for over half of all bone tuberculosis cases. Described by Percivall Pott in 1779, it occurs when Mycobacterium tuberculosis spreads through the Batson venous plexus to seed the vascular cancellous bone of the anterior vertebral body.

vis.alt: Medical diagram of Pott spine showing paradiscal vertebral collapse, gibbus deformity, and cold abscess compressing spinal cord.
vis.caption: Pott spine demonstrating vertebral body collapse, cold abscess formation, and spinal cord compression.

steps.tx: The disease characteristically begins as a **paradiscal lesion**, where caseous granulomatous necrosis destroys the contiguous subchondral bone plates of two adjacent vertebrae and the intervening intervertebral disc. Because mycobacteria produce no proteolytic collagenases, disc destruction occurs secondary to avascular ischemia and mechanical herniation into softened bone, contrasting with rapid pyogenic enzymatic disc dissolution.
steps.say: The infection typically starts in the paradiscal region, eroding the subchondral bone plates of two adjacent vertebrae and the disc between them. Unlike pyogenic bacteria which rapidly melt discs with proteolytic enzymes, tuberculosis destroys the disc slowly through avascular necrosis and collapse.

vis.title: Anatomical Types of Spinal Tuberculosis
rows: Early disc space narrowing; commonest form
Multiple vertebral scalloping without disc loss

steps.tx: Extensive anterior vertebral body collapse under physiological axial weight-bearing produces a sharp, angular kyphotic deformity termed a **gibbus deformity**. The anterior cortical columns crush into a wedge shape while the posterior elements remain intact, creating a prominent dorsal bony prominence. This sharp knuckle-like angular kyphus contrasts distinctly with the smooth, rounded kyphosis seen in rickets or Scheuermann disease.
steps.say: As caseous necrosis rots the anterior vertebral bodies, normal body weight crushes them into wedges, creating a sharp, knuckle-like angular kyphosis known as a gibbus deformity. This sharp backward angle contrasts sharply with the smooth, sweeping curve seen in rickets or Scheuermann kyphosis.

left.title: Tuberculous Gibbus Kyphosis
points: Intact posterior neural arch acts as pivot

right.title: Postural / Scheuermann Curve
points: Absence of cold abscess or bony destruction

steps.tx: A hallmark manifestation is the **cold abscess**, so called because it lacks the classic acute inflammatory signs of warmth, erythema, and acute throbbing pain. Tuberculous caseous pus and necrotic bone debris track along gravity-dependent fascial sheaths. In the thoracic spine, it forms a characteristic fusiform or bird-nest paravertebral abscess, whereas lumbar infection tracks down the psoas sheath to present as a painless swelling in the groin.
steps.say: A cold abscess is an indolent collection of tuberculous pus and dead bone that lacks redness, heat, or throbbing pain. It tracks along fascial planes. In the thoracic spine, it shows up as a fusiform birds nest shadow on chest X-ray. In the lumbar spine, it tracks along the psoas muscle into the groin.

vis.title: Cold Abscess Anatomical Pathways
rows: Fluctuant mass in groin below inguinal ligament
Bulging psoas margin on plain X-ray

steps.tx: The most dreaded neurological sequela is **Pott paraplegia**, occurring in ten to twenty percent of patients due to spinal cord compression by caseous abscess, necrotic sequestra, or severe angular gibbus. Antitubercular therapy using four drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for nine to twelve months constitutes the foundation of treatment. Urgent anterior surgical decompression is indicated for progressive neurological deficits or refractory deformities.
steps.say: Pott paraplegia is spinal cord compression caused by inflammatory pus, dead bone fragments, or severe gibbus wedging. Four-drug antitubercular therapy for nine to twelve months is the foundation of cure. Urgent surgical decompression through an anterior approach is required if neurological deficits worsen despite medical therapy.

left.title: Medical Antitubercular Therapy
points: HRZE for 2 months, followed by HRE for 7 to 10 months
Reverses early paraplegia in >80% of patients
Monitored via ESR and serial MRI scans

right.title: Surgical Decompression (Hong Kong)
points: Refractory cold abscess under high pressure
Severe spinal instability or kyphosis > 40 deg
Anterior debridement and strut bone grafting

quiz.q: What is the commonest anatomical pattern of vertebral involvement in tuberculous spondylitis?
options: Paradiscal pattern affecting contiguous vertebral bodies and the intervening disc
Central vertebral pattern producing isolated vertebra plana
Isolated posterior arch involvement of the spinous process
Synovial facet joint infection without vertebral body involvement
quiz.explain: The paradiscal pattern is the most common form (approx 80%), involving the contiguous subchondral bone plates of two adjacent vertebrae and the intervening intervertebral disc.

quiz.q: Which radiographic sign on an anteroposterior chest radiograph suggests a thoracic cold abscess in Pott spine?
options: Fusiform or bird-nest paravertebral soft tissue shadow
Deep sulcus sign in the costophrenic angle
quiz.explain: In thoracic Pott spine, a cold abscess contained by the endothoracic fascia produces a classic fusiform or bird-nest soft tissue shadow surrounding the collapsed vertebral bodies.
